items.q: In Mitchell's *EnjoySport* task, **Sky** has 3 values and **AirTemp, Humidity, Wind, Water, Forecast** each have 2. How many **semantically distinct** hypotheses does the conjunctive space contain?
items.explain: Each attribute can take its values **or** '?' → $(k_i+1)$ choices: Sky $4$, the other five $3$ each, giving $4\cdot3^5=972$, plus **1** for all the reject-all ($\emptyset$) hypotheses = **973**. (Mitchell, Exercise 2.1.)

items.q: Adding a new attribute $A$ with $k$ possible values to a conjunctive learning task multiplies the number of possible **instances** by $k$ and the number of **hypotheses** by:
items.explain: An extra attribute adds a slot that can be any of its $k$ values **or** '?', i.e. $(k+1)$ choices — so the hypothesis count scales by $k+1$. (Mitchell, Exercise 2.1.)

items.q: With an **unbiased** hypothesis space (the full power set of instances), an unseen instance $x$ matches what fraction of the version space — and what does this imply?
options: Exactly half; the learner cannot generalize to unseen instances (futility of bias-free learning)
None of it; the learner memorizes
items.explain: For the power-set hypothesis space, exactly half the version-space hypotheses label $x$ positive and half negative — so an unbiased learner has **no basis to classify unseen data**. This is Mitchell's *futility of bias-free learning*. (Exercise 2.8.)

options: the most general hypothesis consistent with the data
the most specific hypothesis consistent with the positive examples
items.explain: Find-S walks the general-to-specific lattice upward, returning the **maximally specific** hypothesis consistent with the positive examples. (Mitchell §2.4.)

items.q: In Mitchell's general-to-specific ordering, $\langle ?,?,?,?,?,?\rangle$ is the ___ hypothesis and $\langle\emptyset,\emptyset,\dots\rangle$ is the ___ one.
options: most general (accepts all); most specific (rejects all)
items.explain: All-'?' accepts every instance (most general); all-$\emptyset$ rejects every instance (most specific). The *more-general-than* relation partially orders the hypothesis space. (Mitchell §2.3.)

items.q: Which of these Boolean functions **can** be represented exactly by a decision tree?
options: All of them — including $A\wedge\neg B$, $A\vee(B\wedge C)$, and $A\oplus B$
items.explain: A decision tree is a disjunction of conjunctions and can represent **any** Boolean function (unlike a single perceptron, which fails on XOR). (Mitchell, Exercise 3.1.)

items.q: A collection has 9 positive and 9 negative examples. Its entropy is:
items.explain: A perfectly balanced 50/50 binary split has entropy $-\tfrac12\log_2\tfrac12-\tfrac12\log_2\tfrac12 = 1.0$ — maximal uncertainty. (Mitchell §3.4, Exercise 3.2.)

items.q: ID3 differs from the Candidate-Elimination algorithm in that ID3:
options: finds all hypotheses consistent with the data
searches a complete hypothesis space but outputs a single tree (incomplete search, preference bias)
uses a restriction bias on an incomplete space
items.explain: ID3 searches the *complete* space of trees but greedily commits to **one** hypothesis (preference bias). Candidate-Elimination searches an *incomplete* space but finds **all** consistent hypotheses (restriction bias). (Mitchell, Exercise 3.4 & §3.6.)

items.q: Information gain of attribute $A$ on set $S$ is defined as:
items.explain: Gain = entropy before the split minus the **expected** entropy after: $H(S)-\sum_v\frac{|S_v|}{|S|}H(S_v)$. (Mitchell §3.4.1.)

items.q: Mitchell's definition: hypothesis $h$ overfits the training data if there is an alternative $h'$ such that:
options: $h$ has lower training error but higher error over the full distribution than $h'$
items.explain: Overfitting: $\text{err}_{train}(h)<\text{err}_{train}(h')$ yet $\text{err}_{D}(h)>\text{err}_{D}(h')$ — better on training, worse on the true distribution. (Mitchell §3.7.)

items.q: In **rule post-pruning** (Mitchell), the decision tree is first converted to rules, then each rule is pruned by:
options: removing any precondition whose removal does not worsen estimated accuracy
items.explain: Rule post-pruning drops individual antecedents (preconditions) when doing so doesn't hurt estimated accuracy, then sorts the rules — finer-grained than subtree pruning. (Mitchell §3.7.2.)

items.q: To let ID3 handle a continuous attribute, Mitchell suggests creating a Boolean test $A < c$ where the threshold $c$ is chosen at:
options: midpoints between adjacent examples whose class label differs, picking the max-gain one
items.explain: Sort by the attribute, find adjacent pairs with differing labels, take the **midpoints** as candidate thresholds, and pick the one with highest information gain. (Mitchell §3.7.2.)

items.q: Mitchell notes information gain is **biased toward attributes with many values**. The standard fix is:
options: use the **gain ratio** (normalize gain by the attribute's split information)
items.explain: Gain favours high-arity attributes (they shatter the data). C4.5 divides gain by *split information* to get the **gain ratio**, penalizing many-valued attributes. (Mitchell §3.7.3.)

items.q: k-Nearest-Neighbour is described as an **instance-based / lazy** learner because it:
options: builds a global model at training time
defers all computation until a query arrives, storing the training examples
items.explain: Lazy/instance-based methods store the examples and only compute (find neighbours) at query time — no global model is built. (Mitchell Ch. 8.)

items.q: Mitchell/Alpaydin: a very flexible model that fits the training set almost perfectly but varies wildly across datasets exhibits:
items.explain: Over-flexible models track noise → low bias but **high variance** (overfitting). The remedy is to trade a little bias for much less variance.

items.q: For a heavily imbalanced problem, Alpaydin/Mitchell recommend reporting precision–recall (and ROC/AUC) rather than accuracy because:
options: a trivial majority-class classifier can score high accuracy while catching none of the minority class
items.explain: On skewed data, predicting the majority class everywhere yields high accuracy yet zero recall on the class of interest — so accuracy is misleading; use precision/recall/AUC.
